blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Principal component analysis (PCA) replaces a set of p correlated variables with p new variables, the principal components. Each component is a weighted sum of the standardised originals. The components are uncorrelated with each other, and they are ordered so that the first captures as much of the total variance as possible, the second as much of what remains, and so on. Usually only the first few are kept.

  • An eigenvalue is the variance of one component. With p standardised items, total variance = p, so the proportion of variance explained by a component is its eigenvalue ÷ p.
  • A loading is the correlation between an original item and a component. An item “loads on” a component when this correlation is large. For standardised items, loading = eigenvector weight × √eigenvalue, and the squared loadings on a component add up to its eigenvalue.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: If 20 items are strongly correlated because they tap a few underlying ideas, much of the information is redundant. PCA finds the directions in which the items vary together most and compresses them into a few components. Each component is a weighted combination of the items, so it can be scored for every respondent. (Components are called orthogonal because they are uncorrelated.)

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. With standardised items, Var(a₁z₁ + … + a_pz_p) = ΣᵢΣⱼ aᵢaⱼrᵢⱼ, the variance of a sum (recall §16.3.1.1, Derivation step 1) with correlations in place of covariances. In matrix shorthand this is written aᵀRa, where R is the p × p table (matrix) of correlations and a the list (vector) of weights.
  2. Maximise aᵀRa subject to aᵀa = a₁² + … + a_p² = 1, to stop the weights growing without limit. Setting the derivative of aᵀRa − λ(aᵀa − 1) to zero (the Lagrange-multiplier method; the calculus is beyond this book) gives Ra = λa.
  3. So the weights are an eigenvector of R and the component’s variance is aᵀRa = λ, the matching eigenvalue. The largest eigenvalue gives the first component. The eigenvalues of R sum to its diagonal total (the trace), which is p ones, so p.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Household asset indices, such as the DHS wealth index, are the classic use in public health. Filmer & Pritchett (2001), using Indian data, constructed “a linear index from asset ownership indicators, using principal-components analysis to derive weights.” The illustration below uses a correlation matrix of five binary asset items (electricity, television, mobile phone, motorcycle, bicycle) in 500 households. It is a teaching matrix, not survey data.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Eigenvalues: 2.24, 1.06, 0.69, 0.58, 0.43 (sum 5). The first component explains 2.24 ÷ 5 = 45% of the variance. The first two explain 66%.
  2. Loadings on component 1: electricity 0.77, television 0.82, mobile 0.74, motorcycle 0.66, bicycle −0.04. Squared and summed: 0.585 + 0.674 + 0.542 + 0.432 + 0.001 = 2.24, the first eigenvalue. The four “modern” assets load together. The bicycle does not: in many villages poorer households own bicycles too.
  3. How many components? The Kaiser criterion keeps components with eigenvalue above 1, a common convention (Vyas & Kumaranayake, 2006). Here it keeps two. The second component (eigenvalue 1.06) is essentially the bicycle alone: its loading is 0.96, and no other item loads above 0.33 in absolute value. A lone item forming its own “component” is noise, not a construct. The scree plot (Figure 16.3) shows a sharp bend after component 1. Cattell’s scree test reads the number of components off that bend. Parallel analysis (Horn, 1965) keeps only components whose eigenvalue beats the matching eigenvalue from random data of the same size. Here parallel analysis returns one component: the random-data second eigenvalue is about 1.05–1.06, the same as the observed 1.06. Both methods point to one component.
  4. Is the matrix worth analysing? The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy compares the correlations with the partial correlations. Values near 1 mean the items share common variance. Kaiser’s own labels, quoted in the documentation of R’s psych package, run from “unacceptable” below 0.5 through “miserable” (0.5s), “mediocre” (0.6s), “middling” (0.7s) and “meritorious” (0.8s) to “marvelous” above 0.9. Here overall KMO = 0.72 (“middling”). For the bicycle alone it is 0.37, a sign to drop it. Bartlett’s test of sphericity tests H₀: the correlation matrix is an identity matrix (no correlations at all). χ² = 439.6 on 10 df, p < 0.001, so there is correlation to summarise. With large samples it is usually significant, so it is a low bar.

blocks.alt: Scree plot for five asset items
blocks.caption: Figure 16.3. Scree plot for the five asset items. The first eigenvalue (2.24, 45% of variance) stands well above the rest. The second (1.06) only just crosses the Kaiser line at 1, and the bend after component 1 suggests one component.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(psych)
items <- c("electricity", "television", "mobile", "motorcycle",
           "bicycle")
R <- matrix(c(1.00, 0.55, 0.40,  0.30,  0.05,
              0.55, 1.00, 0.45,  0.40,  0.00,
              0.40, 0.45, 1.00,  0.35,  0.10,
              0.30, 0.40, 0.35,  1.00, -0.10,
              0.05, 0.00, 0.10, -0.10,  1.00),
            nrow = 5, dimnames = list(items, items))
round(eigen(R)$values, 2)
KMO(R)
cortest.bartlett(R, n = 500)
principal(R, nfactors = 1, n.obs = 500)$loadings
[1] 2.24 1.06 0.69 0.58 0.43
...
Overall MSA =  0.72
MSA for each item = 
electricity  television      mobile  motorcycle     bicycle 
       0.72        0.69        0.77        0.76        0.37

eigen gives step 1. KMO and cortest.bartlett give step 4. principal prints the loadings of step 2. The bicycle’s loading (−0.04) is left blank because R hides loadings below 0.1. “SS loadings” is the sum of squared loadings (the eigenvalue, 2.236), and “Proportion Var” is 2.236 ÷ 5 = 0.447.

points.html: Binary items. PCA was designed for continuous variables, yet asset indices routinely run it on binary items (Filmer & Pritchett, 2001). Categorical variables are recoded into binary indicators (Vyas & Kumaranayake, 2006). Critics note that the approach “is statistically inappropriate for use with discrete data” (Howe, Hargreaves & Huttly, 2008). Alternatives are PCA on tetrachoric or polychoric correlations or multiple correspondence analysis.

Rotation. When two or more components are kept, their loadings can be rotated to make them easier to interpret: each item loads highly on one component and near zero on the others. Varimax keeps the components uncorrelated (orthogonal rotation). Promax and oblimin let them correlate (oblique rotation), which suits constructs that are expected to be related, such as sub-domains of quality of life. Rotation redistributes the variance explained among the kept components. It does not change the total.

PCA versus factor analysis. PCA summarises total variance and makes no model of where it comes from. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) models only the shared (common) variance as caused by latent factors and treats the rest as item-specific error. For scale development, EFA matches the idea of a construct causing its indicators more closely. In practice the two often give similar loadings.
PCA checks dimensionality before α is reported (§16.3.1.1). If items split into several components, report α for each sub-scale.
Software names saved component or factor scores automatically. SPSS, for example, names them FAC1_1, FAC2_1 and so on for the first set of saved scores (IBM SPSS FACTOR documentation).
